title: Obon
hookLine: in Japan a summer festival welcoming ancestors home, linked to the story of Moggallana helping his mother (Ullambana)

cards: It's August in Japan. Trains are packed with people going home, to the towns their families come from. At dusk, outside the houses, small fires are lit by the door.
They're welcome fires, called mukaebi, so the spirits of the family's dead can find their way back. For a few days, the ancestors are guests.

This week closed the great collections and stepped into the festival year: the moon calendar, Vesak's lanterns, Mahinda on the mountain, the rains, the tooth on the tusker's back. It closes in Japan, with Obon.

teach.b: Obon, often just called Bon, traces back to a story in a Chinese Buddhist scripture, the Ullambana Sutra.
In it, Moggallana, the disciple well-known for his powers of mind, the same one you saw nodding off and pulling his ears, uses those powers to look for his dead mother.
He finds her reborn among the hungry ghosts, starving.
He brings her a bowl of rice, but as it touches her mouth, it bursts into flame. Heartbroken, he goes to the Buddha.

The Buddha tells him that on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the rains retreat ends, he should make offerings to the whole community of monks; the merit of that gift can reach seven generations of ancestors.
Moggallana does it, and his mother is freed. Scholars note that this scripture appears to have been composed in China, not translated from an Indian original; it doesn't appear in the Pali canon.
But it shaped festivals across East Asia.

In Japan, families clean graves, set out food and flowers at home altars, and invite a priest to chant. In the evenings, whole neighborhoods dance the Bon Odori in circles, some say born from Moggallana's joy.
At the end, the spirits are sent off with farewell fires, like the giant characters lit on the mountains around Kyoto, or with paper lanterns floated down rivers to the sea.
For a few days, the dead are family at the table.

how: During Obon, Japanese families return to their hometowns, clean and visit graves, make offerings at home altars, invite priests to chant, dance the Bon Odori, and light fires or float lanterns to welcome and send off ancestors.

o: a Japanese new year of cleaning and visits
Japan's summer festival welcoming the dead home
Japan's spring festival of cherry blossoms

scholars think it was composed in China; it's not in the Pali canon.

games.q: you're Moggallana. your mother is starving among the hungry ghosts, and the rice you bring bursts into flame. what do you do?
o: go to the Buddha for help.
games.why: he goes to the Buddha, who tells him to make offerings to the whole community at the end of the rains. through that gift, his mother is freed.

practice: Light a candle if you have one, or picture one, and let its glow settle you.
Bring to mind someone in your family who has died, a grandparent, a parent, someone further back whose name you only heard; if none comes, think of all the people who came before you.
Welcome them in your own way, say a name inwardly, and stay a little.

wordCard.voice: Obon. Japan's summer festival of the dead, when ancestors are welcomed home with fires, food and dancing, rooted in the story of Moggallana and his mother. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese obon: the festival's name, a shortened, honorific form of urabon, from Ullambana.

carryVoice: Your line: they come home. Welcomed with fire, sent off with light. Rest well tonight.
